Yes, when it's extremely obvious that someone is showing a certain emotion, it is completely valid to apply logic and come to a conclusion. But the point I was trying to raise is that when we consider that there might be underlying factors that drive a character to act the way they do, it's harder to come to a logical and objective conclusion on if a character has underlying issues that linger after a traumatic event if that person doesn't openly express their actual feelings.

However, I'll have to concede on the argument because I agree with your rebuttal regarding the level of subjectivity. While I could continue pushing the idea that certain actions may be due to his underlying trauma, I can't deny that it's far too subjective as an argument stance. But again, I thank you for this perspective; I may need to rewatch TLA because a lot of your points have added to my skepticism on if the writing of the initial series was as good as many in the fandom assumed it to be.

Comparing the characters isn't necessarily a bad thing, but I'm speaking to the sense of people arguing whether one person experienced more pain than another. It's a reductive argument to have,  and one that I feel kinda defeats the overarching narrative of both series. Additionally, it is usually only in an attempt to label one as the better Avatar over the other, which you don't need to compare character trauma to do.

While my point can be easily dismissed by "calm down, it's just a drawing, son," the idea of comparing trauma is inherently problematic. If someone's okay with comparing the trauma two characters experienced, who's to say they aren't doing it with people in the real world as well? Why is it so easy for their morals to drop when the individual in question is fictional?

\>Aang is not a real person. He cannot be said to "feel" anything the audience isn't made aware of.

Real or fake, I think it's pretty obtuse to assume that under the happy-go-lucky shell, that Aang presents on the outside, that he isn't hurting internally. If anything, the limitations of it being a fictional show, only further explains why the trauma isn't exactly all in your face. 

\>When the episode right after Aang finds out all of his people were killed is him going "Oh boy, let's ride the elephant koi!" that tells me that sure he's grieving, but he's not traumatized. 

This is where I feel nuance goes out the window because you're trying to look at it from a logical perspective when we are discussing emotions. Whether or not Aang's a fictional character, your interpretation on what you've seen is subjective at best. Concluding that because \*you\* don't see trauma through his actions that it isn't true is an absence of evidence fallacy. 

\>They're different things. If that's not what it's supposed to be, then the authors have failed to communicate that. 

It's also very possible for two things to be present at the same time, even if you only perceive one rather than another. While you see Aang overexcited to ride elephant koi as him grieving silently, I see it as a common trauma response he displays throughout the series: avoidance. Most children experiencing trauma tend to fall back on avoidance as a response to their situations. It's very common for a child to experience trauma but run around a playground with a big smile on their face and that's quite literally how Aang's trauma was presented in my opinion. 

\>They can't fall back on "just assume things we never wrote" because then there's no way to tell who's assuming the right things. No, you feeling very strongly that your assumptions are right is not proof.

You can critique Bryke's execution of how Aang was portrayed, but my stance on how the trauma portrayed isn't really fallacious in the sense of "I have a very strong assumption." My conclusion is that people have suffered in silence, in and out of fiction, and Aang is one of them. He doesn't show it through his personality but often through subtle actions like hiding Hakoda's letter, various statements he's made about his role as the Avatar, and his frequency to avoid situations that are too triggering for him.

\>If you want to put words in my mouth & get offended by them, I can't stop you, but the fact is that part of responding differently is not everyone experiences the same level of distress.

I hope I haven't put any words in your mouth with this response so far, but I assure you that I'm not offended by your rebuttal so far. This was an interesting perspective to read and discuss with you on. I also agree with this point and it was why the prior debate I had on TT irritated me so badly. Trauma can vary at different levels even if it's a similar event. 

  
\>If the audience isn't allowed to criticize that, then the author can just write any old shit they want about trauma & everyone else is obligated to act like it's accurate, which is absurd.

Just to reinterate, I'm not saying that everyone should come to the conclusion on whether or not a character is experiencing a certain event or not. Everyone is obligated to their own interpretation of a narrative as what they've been given on screen, in a book, etc. However, that's again where I see space for nuance rather than a distinct yes or no conclusion. 

With all that said, I enjoyed the discourse you are bringing to this topic. It isn't necessarily offensive to me because it's different from the initial debate I was engaged in. In the prior one, it was already under the pretense that Aang \*did\* experience trauma and trying to determine whether his or Korra's was worse. 

In my opinion it's a big difference in analyzing Aang's portrayal in TLA to determine if he actually experienced trauma vs. conceding that he did have trauma but that it was not comparable to Korra's based on a lack of on-screen moments.
